people.name: Luis Garzón
people.dates: Born about 1867; death year not found
body: In 1886 a nineteen-year-old oboe player from Mexico City came to Minneapolis with a touring Mexican band. Luis Garzón fell ill there, and the band moved on without him. He stayed, married a local woman, and spent most of the rest of his life in the Twin Cities. The Minnesota Historical Society's MNopedia calls him the first Latino to make a permanent home in Minnesota.
He made his living in music at first. The Ramsey County Historical Society's journal reports that he joined the Minneapolis Symphony Orchestra and played with theater orchestras and community bands.

In the following decades Mexican and Mexican American newcomers came north, many to work the sugar beet farms of rural Minnesota, and many settled on St. Paul's West Side. In the early 1920s Garzón opened a grocery there, a bright blue store on East Fairfield Street in the river flats. A St. Paul Pioneer Press reporter wrote in 1928 that sooner or later every Mexican who stayed for any length of time in St. Paul came to the store, and that it worked as a grocery, business office, information bureau and club room.

That same year Garzón and other neighborhood leaders were promoting a social club to bring newcomers together, involve them in city affairs and keep Mexican culture alive. His life later inspired the chamber opera Tienda, by composer Reinaldo Moya and lyricist Caitlin Vincent, which premiered at Augsburg University in 2020 and was later presented by the Schubert Club.
keyFacts: 1886: Arrives in Minneapolis at nineteen with a touring Mexican band and stays after falling ill.
Plays with the Minneapolis Symphony Orchestra, theater orchestras and community bands.
Early 1920s: Opens a grocery on St. Paul's West Side.
1928: The St. Paul Pioneer Press describes the store as a hub for Mexican residents of St. Paul.
2020: The chamber opera Tienda premieres at Augsburg University.

people.name: Irene Gomez-Bethke
people.field: Civil rights, state government, arts and culture
body: In 1982 Governor Rudy Perpich appointed a Minneapolis-born Chicana activist to run the Minnesota Department of Human Rights. The department had a backlog of about 3,000 cases, and Irene Gomez-Bethke developed the plan that eliminated it. For people waiting to be heard on complaints of unfair treatment at work, in housing or in public life, that meant their cases finally moved.

She was born Irene Marie Gomez in Minneapolis in 1935, the second of six children of Jesse and Maria Gomez, who had immigrated from Mexico. Chicano and Chicana are terms that many Mexican Americans took up in the civil rights era of the 1960s and 1970s, and she used the word for herself.

In 1974 she helped found Centro Cultural Chicano in Minneapolis. She then helped found the Instituto de Arte y Cultura and served as its executive director, and in that role she introduced Hispanic Heritage Month to Minnesota. She twice chaired the Hispanic Advisory Committee to the Minneapolis mayor. Her work joined culture and civil rights: art, music and celebration brought people together and made them visible, and visibility helped them press for fair treatment.

She married Jack Arthur Bethke in 1953 and raised six children. She retired from public life in 2001 and gave her papers to the Minnesota Historical Society. She died on March 21, 2021, survived by six children, 14 grandchildren and 21 great-grandchildren.
keyFacts: 1935: Born in Minneapolis to parents who immigrated from Mexico.
1974: Helps found Centro Cultural Chicano in Minneapolis.
1982: Appointed Minnesota Commissioner of Human Rights; her plan eliminates a backlog of about 3,000 cases.
Helps found and directs the Instituto de Arte y Cultura; introduces Hispanic Heritage Month to Minnesota.
March 21, 2021: Dies. Her papers (1970–2001) are at the Minnesota Historical Society.

people.name: Conrado "Conrad" Vega
body: When the Minnesota Senate convened in January 1977, one of its new members was a social studies teacher from Lakeville High School. Conrad Vega, a DFLer from Dakota County, is recorded by the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library as the first known Hispanic person to serve in the Minnesota Legislature.
Vega was born on June 22, 1938, in South St. Paul, and was of Mexican ancestry. South St. Paul's stockyards and meatpacking plants long drew working families to the city.

Voters elected him to the Senate in 1976. He served from 1977 to 1986, representing District 52 and then, after redistricting, District 39. He also served on the South St. Paul Economic Development Authority. He died on December 26, 2010, at age 72.
keyFacts: June 22, 1938: Born in South St. Paul. Of Mexican ancestry.
Teaches social studies at Lakeville High School.
1976: Elected to the Minnesota Senate. Takes office in 1977 as the first known Hispanic legislator in Minnesota.
1977–1986: Represents District 52 (1977–1982) and District 39 (1983–1986).
December 26, 2010: Dies at age 72.

people.name: Patricia Torres Ray
body: In November 2006, voters in a Minneapolis Senate district elected Patricia Torres Ray. She became the first Latina elected to the Minnesota Senate. Sahan Journal calls her the first Latina elected to the Legislature, while MNopedia names Edwina Garcia as the first Latina in the Legislature, with 1991 in the body of its entry and 1998 in its chronology.

She was born on March 25, 1964, in Pasto, a city in the Andes of southern Colombia, where she also studied law. In Minnesota she earned a bachelor's degree in urban studies from the University of Minnesota and, in 2004, a master's in public affairs from the Humphrey Institute.

She served in the Senate from 2007 until January 2023, representing District 62 and then District 63. She was majority whip in her first two sessions and later chaired the Education and the State and Local Government committees. In 2010 a state senator running for governor named her his running mate for lieutenant governor; the Minneapolis Foundation describes her as the first woman of color to run for that office in Minnesota. He withdrew at the DFL convention. In 2018 she ran for Congress in the Fifth District and lost the DFL primary.

She did not seek re-election in 2022. As of the most recent accounts found, from 2023 and 2024, she runs PTR Associates, which helps small organizations with political and policy strategy, and she was named a Minneapolis Foundation trustee in 2023.
keyFacts: March 25, 1964: Born in Pasto, Colombia.
2004: Master's degree, Humphrey Institute.
2006: Elected the first Latina member of the Minnesota Senate; serves 2007 to 2023.
2010: Named a gubernatorial candidate's running mate for lieutenant governor.
2018: Runs for Congress in the Fifth District and loses the primary.
After leaving office: Runs PTR Associates.
people.connectToWork: "Latino" covers many national origins and many generations. What do your forms and reports treat as one group, and what does that hide about who you serve?

people.name: Melisa López Franzen
body: In September 2021 the Minnesota Senate DFL caucus chose a new leader, Melisa López Franzen, a senator from Edina. A 2021 Minnesota Reformer report cited by the Legislative Reference Library describes her as the first Latina and first person of color to lead a legislative caucus in Minnesota.

She was born on June 9, 1980, and grew up in Puerto Rico, attending high school in Aguadilla on the island's northwest coast. People born in Puerto Rico are U.S. citizens by birth, so a move to the mainland is migration within the country, not immigration. She earned a bachelor's degree from the Interamerican University of Puerto Rico, then a master's in public policy from the University of Minnesota's Humphrey Institute and, in 2006, a law degree from Hamline University School of Law.

She was elected to the Minnesota Senate in 2012 and represented District 49 from 2013 to 2023. She led her caucus as minority leader and did not seek re-election in 2022. She was president of NewPublica, a Hispanic-owned public relations firm. She joined the University of Minnesota in August 2023 as executive director of government and community relations, and in February 2025 the University's president announced that she had decided to leave. In 2025 she entered the DFL race for an open U.S. Senate seat and ended her campaign that May. The sources checked in October 2026 name no later role.
keyFacts: June 9, 1980: Born. Grows up in Puerto Rico.
2006: Law degree, Hamline University School of Law.
2012: Elected to the Minnesota Senate; serves 2013 to 2023.
September 13, 2021: Elected Senate DFL minority leader.
August 2023: Joins the University of Minnesota as executive director of government and community relations.
February 2025: The University announces she has decided to leave.
May 2025: Ends her campaign for U.S. Senate.

people.name: Jimmy Longoria
body: On summer days in Minneapolis neighborhoods, Jimmy Longoria has worked alongside young people painting large, brightly colored murals meant to deter graffiti and gangs. He runs the effort, Mentoring Peace Through Art, with his wife, Connie Longoria Fullmer.

He was raised on a small South Texas farm in an extended Tejano family. He chose to call himself a Chicano artist in 1974, which tied him to the Chicano art movement that grew out of the Mexican American civil rights struggles of the 1960s and 1970s. He switched his studies to art at Pitzer College in California, then worked in Los Angeles and Chicago.

He moved to Minnesota in 1988 for a day job and stayed. He received a Bush Foundation Artist Fellowship in 2010, and MPR News reports that he has made his living solely as an artist since then. His four-panel painting Native Girl Lost was installed at the Bush Foundation's St. Paul offices in 2015, and 3M's Innovation Center commissioned art from him using its products. MPR News reports that his work hangs in the homes and offices of Justice Sonia Sotomayor and the actor and collector Cheech Marin. At 70, in 2024, he was still painting.
keyFacts: Raised in South Texas. Reported as 70 in 2024.
1974: Commits to identifying as a Chicano artist.
1988: Moves to Minnesota.
Runs Mentoring Peace Through Art with his wife, leading youth mural projects in Minneapolis.
2010: Bush Foundation Artist Fellowship.
2015: Native Girl Lost installed at the Bush Foundation, St. Paul.

people.name: Edwina Garcia
people.field: State and city government, student advising
body: When the Minnesota House of Representatives opened its 1991 session, one of its new members was a Richfield city council veteran who worked as a counselor at the University of Minnesota's Chicano-Latino Resource Center. Edwina Garcia, a DFLer, is recorded by the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library as the first known Hispanic woman, and the first known woman from an ethnic minority group, to serve in the Minnesota Legislature.

She was born in December 1944 in Clovis, New Mexico, a state where Hispanic families were living long before it became part of the United States. She moved from Clovis to Richfield in 1971 and advised Hispanic students at the University of Minnesota.

Her public career started locally. She served on Richfield's Housing and Redevelopment Authority, its Human Rights Commission and other city commissions, and on the Richfield City Council from 1986 to 1990. In the state House she served from 1991 to 1998, first in District 40A and then in District 63B. In 1998 she won the DFL primary for Secretary of State and lost the general election to Republican Mary Kiffmeyer. In 2002 she ran for the state Senate in District 63 as the Independence Party nominee and lost.
keyFacts: December 1944: Born in Clovis, New Mexico.
1971: Moves to Richfield.
Works as a Hispanic student advisor and counselor at the University of Minnesota.
1986–1990: Serves on the Richfield City Council.
1991–1998: Minnesota House, the first known Hispanic woman in the Minnesota Legislature.
1998: Wins the DFL primary for Secretary of State; loses the general election.

people.name: Dolores Huerta
body: In 1955, through the Community Service Organization in Stockton, California, a young organizer named Dolores Huerta met another organizer, César Chávez. In 1962 the two left the organization and founded the National Farm Workers Association, which became the United Farm Workers. Farmworkers at that time were excluded from the federal law that protected other workers' right to organize.

In March 2026 a New York Times investigation, as reported locally, alleged that Chávez sexually assaulted girls and women. Huerta confirmed the allegations and was described as one of those abused, according to the West St. Paul Reader. Minnesota repealed Cesar Chavez Day through Laws 2026, Chapter 42, signed March 27, 2026, and the governor proclaimed March 31, 2026, Farmworkers Day.

She was born Dolores Clara Fernández on April 10, 1930, in Dawson, New Mexico, and moved with her mother and brothers to Stockton after her parents divorced. She worked as a teacher of farmworkers' children and was moved by students who came to school hungry and without shoes. That experience turned her toward organizing.

She became one of the movement's key negotiators and strategists. She won contracts with growers, organized during the 1965 Delano grape strike, and helped lead boycotts that asked consumers across the country to stop buying table grapes. By the account of the foundation she started, she helped win disability insurance and public assistance benefits for farmworkers in 1963 and was instrumental in passing California's Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975. Her slogan "¡Sí, se puede!" ("Yes, we can!") spread far beyond farm labor. In 2012 President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
She kept organizing through the Dolores Huerta Foundation. She died of cancer at her home in Bakersfield, California, on October 28, 2026, at age 96, according to a family spokesperson.
keyFacts: April 10, 1930: Born in Dawson, New Mexico. Raised in Stockton, California.
1955: Meets César Chávez through the Community Service Organization.
1962: Co-founds the National Farm Workers Association.
1975: Helps pass California's Agricultural Labor Relations Act.
2012: Receives the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
October 28, 2026: Dies at home in Bakersfield, California, at age 96.

people.name: Ellen Ochoa
body: In April 1993 the space shuttle Discovery lifted off on mission STS-56 to study Earth's ozone layer. On board was Ellen Ochoa, an electrical engineer and inventor, who became the first Hispanic woman to travel to space.

She was born in 1958 in Los Angeles and grew up in La Mesa, California. She graduated from Grossmont High School in 1975 as valedictorian, earned a bachelor's degree in physics from San Diego State University in 1980, then a master's in 1981 and, in 1985, a doctorate in electrical engineering from Stanford University. Before joining NASA she was a research engineer working on optical systems, and she is a co-inventor on three patents.

NASA selected her as an astronaut in 1990. Over four shuttle flights she logged nearly 1,000 hours in orbit. She then moved into leadership at Johnson Space Center in Houston, serving as deputy director of Flight Crew Operations and later as the center's deputy director. In 2013 she became director, the center's first Hispanic director and its second woman director, and she led it until 2018. She is also a classical flutist who played in the Stanford Symphony Orchestra.
keyFacts: 1958: Born in Los Angeles. Grows up in La Mesa, California.
1985: Ph.D. in electrical engineering, Stanford. Co-inventor on three patents.
1990: Selected by NASA as an astronaut.
April 1993: Flies on STS-56, the first Hispanic woman in space. Flies four missions in all.
2013–2018: Director of NASA's Johnson Space Center.

people.name: Julia Alvarez
body: In 1960, when Julia Alvarez was ten years old, her family fled the Dominican Republic for New York. Her father had been linked to a failed plot against the dictator Rafael Trujillo. Four months after they left, Trujillo's regime assassinated three of the Mirabal sisters, activists who had opposed him. Decades later Alvarez would tell their story to the world.

She was born in New York City on March 27, 1950, and her family returned to the Dominican Republic when she was about three months old. She spent her childhood under the Trujillo dictatorship. Arriving in New York at ten meant learning a new language and facing a culture that did not always welcome her.

She became a poet, novelist and professor. She graduated from Middlebury College in 1971, later taught in its English department and was its writer-in-residence until 2016. Her 1991 novel How the García Girls Lost Their Accents follows four Dominican sisters adjusting to life in the United States. Her 1994 novel In the Time of the Butterflies imagines the lives of the Mirabal sisters; its publisher reports more than a million copies sold, and it was adapted into a 2001 film and chosen for the National Endowment for the Arts' Big Read. In 2013 she received the National Medal of Arts. Her other honors include the Pura Belpré Award and the Hispanic Heritage Award in Literature.
keyFacts: March 27, 1950: Born in New York City. Raised in the Dominican Republic.
1960: Family flees the Trujillo dictatorship for the United States.
1991: Publishes How the García Girls Lost Their Accents.
1994: Publishes In the Time of the Butterflies.
2013: Receives the National Medal of Arts.

people.name: Roberto Clemente
body: On September 30, 1972, at Three Rivers Stadium in Pittsburgh, Roberto Clemente lined a double against the New York Mets. It was his 3,000th regular-season hit, making him only the eleventh major leaguer to reach that mark. It was also his last regular-season hit. Three months later he was gone.

He was born on August 18, 1934, in Carolina, Puerto Rico, and played all 18 of his seasons with the Pittsburgh Pirates, from 1955 to 1972. He helped lead Pittsburgh to World Series titles in 1960 and 1971, when he hit .414 and was named Series MVP. In those years Latin American and Black players faced segregation, especially in spring training in the South, and mockery of their accents in the press. Clemente spoke out against that treatment.

Off the field he devoted himself to service, especially in Puerto Rico and Latin America. In December 1972 a devastating earthquake struck Managua, Nicaragua. When he learned that relief supplies were not reaching survivors, he decided to deliver them himself. On December 31, 1972, the overloaded plane carrying him and the supplies crashed off the coast of Puerto Rico, and his body was never recovered.

In 1973 the Baseball Hall of Fame held a special election that waived its usual five-year wait and elected him, the first Latin American player inducted. The Pirates retired his number 21. Major League Baseball's Roberto Clemente Award now honors players for character and community work.
keyFacts: August 18, 1934: Born in Carolina, Puerto Rico.
1955–1972: Plays 18 seasons for the Pittsburgh Pirates; 1971 World Series MVP.
September 30, 1972: Records his 3,000th regular-season hit.
December 31, 1972: Dies in a plane crash while bringing earthquake relief to Nicaragua.
1973: Elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame by special election.

people.name: Antonia Novello
body: In 1990 a pediatrician from Puerto Rico became the nation's doctor. President George H. W. Bush appointed Antonia Novello Surgeon General of the United States. She was the first woman, and the first Hispanic person, to hold the office.

She was born Antonia Coello in Fajardo, Puerto Rico. Her father died when she was four, and her mother, a high school principal, raised her. As a child she lived with a chronic condition that sent her to the hospital again and again, until surgeries at 18 and 20 corrected it. Being a patient helped shape her decision, as a teenager, to become a doctor.

She earned her medical degree at the University of Puerto Rico, trained in kidney medicine at the University of Michigan, where she was the first woman named Intern of the Year, and earned a public health degree from Johns Hopkins in 1982. In 1978 she joined the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps and went to work at the National Institutes of Health, rising to deputy director of the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, where she focused on pediatric AIDS. On assignment to a Senate committee she helped draft the organ transplant procurement law of 1984.

As Surgeon General she focused on the health of young people, women and minorities, taking on underage drinking, smoking, AIDS, childhood immunization and health care for Hispanic communities. She is remembered especially for her campaign against tobacco advertising aimed at children, including the Joe Camel ads. She later served as a UNICEF special representative (1993–1996), taught health policy at Johns Hopkins, and in 1999 was nominated as New York State Commissioner of Health.
keyFacts: Born Antonia Coello in Fajardo, Puerto Rico.
1978: Joins the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps and NIH.
1990: Appointed Surgeon General, the first woman and first Hispanic person in the post.
1993–1996: UNICEF special representative.
1999: Nominated New York State Commissioner of Health.

people.name: Roy P. Benavidez
body: On May 2, 1968, near Loc Ninh, Vietnam, a 12-man Special Forces reconnaissance team was trapped under heavy enemy fire. Staff Sergeant Roy Benavidez volunteered to go in on a rescue helicopter. Over the next hours, severely wounded, he directed the troops, recovered classified documents and helped load the dead and wounded. When the helicopter crashed after its pilot was mortally wounded, he called in aircraft for a second extraction. At least eight men were saved. The Army records that he suffered seven major gunshot wounds and 28 shrapnel wounds.

He was born on August 5, 1935, in Lindenau near Cuero, Texas, and grew up around El Campo. By the Army's account his father was Mexican American and his mother Native American. Both parents died of tuberculosis, and his grandfather, aunt and uncle raised him. He left school as a teenager to help support his family, joined the Texas Army National Guard in 1952 and went on active duty in 1955.

He received the Distinguished Service Cross on July 24, 1968. His commander twice recommended him for the Medal of Honor without success; it took added eyewitness testimony before the case was approved. On February 24, 1981, President Ronald Reagan presented him the Medal of Honor at the Pentagon. He worked on veterans' issues and spoke often at schools and civic groups. He died on November 29, 1998, at Brooke Army Medical Center in San Antonio, at 63.
keyFacts: August 5, 1935: Born near Cuero, Texas.
May 2, 1968: Rescue near Loc Ninh, Vietnam; at least eight men saved.
July 24, 1968: Distinguished Service Cross.
February 24, 1981: Medal of Honor from President Reagan.
November 29, 1998: Dies in San Antonio.

people.name: Bill Richardson
body: In 1995 a U.S. congressman sat down face to face with Saddam Hussein and won the release of two American aerospace workers held in Iraq. It was one of many such missions for Bill Richardson, who became one of the best-known American negotiators for people held abroad.

He was born on November 15, 1947, in Pasadena, California, to a Mexican mother and an American bank executive father, and grew up in Mexico City before being sent at 13 to school in Massachusetts. He earned a bachelor's degree from Tufts University in 1970 and a master's from its Fletcher School in 1971.

He represented New Mexico in the U.S. House from 1983 to 1997. President Clinton named him U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations (1997–1998) and then Secretary of Energy (1998–2001). He was governor of New Mexico from 2003 to 2011 and ran for the 2008 Democratic presidential nomination. Through the Richardson Center he kept negotiating for detained Americans, and in 2021 he secured the release of journalist Danny Fenster from prison in Myanmar. He died in his sleep on September 1, 2023, at his home in Chatham, Massachusetts.
keyFacts: November 15, 1947: Born in Pasadena, California; raised in Mexico City.
1983–1997: U.S. Representative from New Mexico.
1997–1998: U.N. Ambassador. 1998–2001: Secretary of Energy.
2003–2011: Governor of New Mexico.
1995 Iraq and 2021 Myanmar: detainee releases.
September 1, 2023: Dies in Chatham, Massachusetts.

people.name: Tito Puente
body: Tito Puente was born Ernest Anthony Puente Jr. on April 20, 1923, in New York City to Puerto Rican parents and grew up in Spanish Harlem. He would become known as El Rey de los Timbales, the King of the Timbales, the paired metal drums at the heart of Latin dance bands.
Drafted by the U.S. Navy in 1942, he served through World War II aboard the escort carrier USS Santee. After the war the G.I. Bill paid for him to study at the Juilliard School.

He went on to lead one of the defining bands of the mambo era in New York. His 1958 album Dance Mania became a classic. His song "Oye Como Va," written and recorded in 1962, later became a rock hit for Carlos Santana. He kept performing for decades. President Clinton's statement at his death counted five Grammy Awards, and he received the National Medal of Arts in 1997. He died on May 31, 2000, in New York City, after heart surgery. In 2003 he received a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.
keyFacts: April 20, 1923: Born in New York City to Puerto Rican parents.

people.name: Isabel Allende
body: In 1981, living in exile in Venezuela, Isabel Allende began writing a letter to her dying grandfather. The letter grew into a novel, The House of the Spirits, published in Spanish in 1982 and in English in 1985.

A Chilean American writer, she was born on August 2, 1942, in Lima, Peru. After Chile's 1973 military coup she was blacklisted, and in 1975 she emigrated to Venezuela with her husband and children. Exile became a theme in her writing.

She has lived in the San Francisco Bay Area since 1987 and became a U.S. citizen in 1993. In December 1996 she launched the Isabel Allende Foundation in honor of her daughter Paula, who had died. In 2014 President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and in 2018 she received the National Book Foundation's Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters. Her own timeline shows her publishing and touring through 2025.
keyFacts: August 2, 1942: Born in Lima, Peru.
1975: Emigrates to Venezuela after being blacklisted following the 1973 coup in Chile.
1982: The House of the Spirits published.
1993: Becomes a U.S. citizen.
1996: Founds the Isabel Allende Foundation.
2014: Presidential Medal of Freedom.

people.name: Conchita Hernández Legorreta
people.field: Disability rights, education of blind students
body: As a blind child in California whose parents faced language barriers, Conchita Hernández Legorreta was often the one translating legal paperwork about her own education, including Individualized Education Program documents she did not yet fully understand. She has described herself as a blind, undocumented Latina immigrant.

She was born in Mexico and grew up in California. She earned a bachelor's degree from Saint Mary's College of California, a master's in teaching from Louisiana Tech University focused on blind students, a certificate in working with DeafBlind students from Northern Illinois University and a doctorate in special education from George Washington University.

In 2016 she co-founded METAS (Mentoring Engaging and Teaching All Students), frustrated that mainstream organizations were not serving communities of color. It is led by disabled professionals of color, trains educators in Latin America who work with blind and low-vision students, and supports Spanish-speaking families in the U.S. She also co-founded the National Coalition for Latinxs with Disabilities and has worked as a Blind and Low Vision Specialist in Maryland. President Biden appointed her to the National Board for Education Sciences.

Her argument is direct. Writing in Refinery29 in 2020, she rejected the idea that the Latinx community has an inherently negative view of disability: "we are not inherently more ableist." She wrote that institutional power controls who has access to information, and that the failure lies with the government, organizations and nonprofits that underserve communities of color and communities in poverty.
keyFacts: Born in Mexico; raised in California.
2016: Co-founds METAS.
Co-founds the National Coalition for Latinxs with Disabilities.
Appointed by President Biden to the National Board for Education Sciences.

people.name: Victor Santiago Pineda
body: Victor Santiago Pineda was born in Venezuela. He told UC Berkeley's business school that he stopped walking at seven, and that he was using a ventilator by the time the Americans with Disabilities Act passed in 1990. A disability organization's profile says he was diagnosed with muscular dystrophy at seven, and that he helped draft the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities as its youngest government delegate.

He holds bachelor's and master's degrees from UC Berkeley and a Ph.D. from UCLA. In 2003 he founded World Enabled and the Pineda Foundation, which work on the rights and dignity of disabled people and on making cities more accessible. He directs the Inclusive Cities Lab at UC Berkeley.

In 2015 President Barack Obama appointed him to the U.S. Access Board, which sets federal accessibility standards. His honors include a Fulbright-Hays Scholarship and the American Association of People with Disabilities' Paul G. Hearne Leadership Award.

2003: Founds World Enabled and the Pineda Foundation.

institutions.name: Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio
institutions.location: St. Paul (headquarters, 797 East 7th Street), Minneapolis, Willmar and Austin, Minnesota
body: The sources give two starting points. MNopedia traces CLUES to 1977, when a Latino graduate student wanted culturally and linguistically appropriate social services for Twin Cities Latinos, and says it began as an association of Latino professionals and incorporated in 1981 with four staff. CLUES itself dates its founding to 1981, on St. Paul's West Side, as Chicanos Latinos Unidos en Servicio. It took its current name in 2005.

CLUES now reports more than 140 employees and more than 700 volunteers. Besides its St. Paul headquarters it has sites in Minneapolis, including the Abriendo Caminos behavioral health clinic and a CareerForce location, and offices in Willmar and Austin, which opened in 2017. Liliana Letran-Garcia became President and CEO on Feb. 2, 2026. Its programs include behavioral health, career training, classes, early childhood and parenting programs, community health, elder programs, survivor advocacy, youth programs, and arts and culture. MNopedia gives 1987 for CLUES helping form HACER, a community research organization, while HACER's own site says it was founded in 1988.
keyFacts: 1977: Roots, by MNopedia's account.
1981: Founded as Chicanos Latinos Unidos en Servicio.
2005: Takes its current name.
Today: More than 140 employees and 700 volunteers, by its own count.

institutions.name: Mercado Central
institutions.type: Cooperative market and small business hub
body: In the early 1990s, members of a Spanish-speaking Catholic congregation in Minneapolis wanted a place where Latino entrepreneurs could start and grow businesses. MNopedia names the congregation Sagrado Corazón de Jesús; Sahan Journal describes organizer Juan Linares's work with the Spanish-speaking congregation at St. Stephen's Catholic Church. Entrepreneurship classes through the Neighborhood Development Center and the Whittier Community Development Corporation turned the idea into a plan, and Project for Pride in Living redeveloped a run-down 28,000-square-foot complex at Lake Street and Bloomington Avenue. The market opened in July 1999 with 47 small businesses, by Sahan Journal's count; a MNopedia caption says 45 Latino-owned businesses, and a 2009 state report says 45 with over $12 million in sales.

Founding business owners bought shares, and tenants rented with an option to own. In 2019 the Cooperativa Mercado Central, a board of vendors, took full ownership. In February 2025 the city forgave a $276,500 loan to the market. In 2025 vendors told Sahan Journal that immigration enforcement had reduced foot traffic and sales. MNopedia calls the market a center of economic and cultural activity.
keyFacts: Early 1990s: Organizing begins through a Spanish-speaking congregation and entrepreneurship classes.
July 1999: Opens at 1515 East Lake Street with 47 businesses by Sahan Journal's count (MNopedia and a 2009 state report say 45).
2019: Vendor cooperative takes full ownership.
February 2025: City forgives a $276,500 loan.

institutions.name: Teatro del Pueblo
institutions.location: 209 West Page Street, St. Paul (West Side)
body: Latino artists and community members on St. Paul's West Side founded Teatro del Pueblo in 1992. By the company's account, an early production about a local school shooting established it as a forum for community voices and won over people who had been skeptical.

The company reports staging more than 50 plays in a fifteen-year span and touring to more than 50 Minnesota schools. Its programs include a Political Theater series curated by co-founder and artistic director Alberto Justiniano, launched as a festival in March 2002, and a Latino/Asian Fusion series developed with Pangea World Theater. It describes itself as the only professional Latino theater company providing artistic and educational programming in Minnesota. As of October 2026 its home page promotes a current podcast season and a Heritage Month music offering and shows no dated production, and it lists no upcoming events.
keyFacts: 1992: Founded on St. Paul's West Side.
March 2002: Political Theater Festival launches.
More than 50 plays and more than 50 school tours, by its own count.
Latino/Asian Fusion series with Pangea World Theater.

institutions.name: discapacitados abriéndose caminos (d.a.c.)
body: d.a.c. is a Spanish- and English-language family center whose tagline is "Luchando juntos y sin limites por nuestros niños." Its website says it guides children and adults with disabilities and their families through the health system, county public services, schools and the community, so that they get the support they need. It lists a phone number, (651) 293-1748.

It is one of the few Minnesota organizations found that is both Spanish-language and specific to disability. As of October 2026 its website is online but shows no dated items and a 2015 footer, so current operation could not be confirmed. Call to learn what it offers now before offering it as a referral.

institutions.name: PACER Center, Latino family autism project
institutions.type: Parent center and state-funded peer support project
body: PACER Center is a Minnesota parent center for families of children with disabilities. In July 2024 it announced a 16-month project funded by the Minnesota Department of Human Services, with Family Voices of Minnesota, for Latino and Somali families of children with disabilities such as autism.

The project included parent support groups led by Latino and Somali staff in each group's language, training for parent volunteers to help others find resources, and tip sheets and videos in English, Spanish and Somali on special education and health care. The 16 months have since passed. Ask PACER what continues.
keyFacts: Announced July 17, 2024.
16-month grant from the Minnesota Department of Human Services.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Latino here covers people with roots in many countries, including Indigenous people from Latin America who may not speak Spanish, and people whose families have been in the United States for generations. No study of how Latino Minnesotans with disabilities or their families understand disability was found. The research below is limited: mostly older, small U.S. studies of Mexican-origin and Puerto Rican parents of young children, plus one study from a related field.
questions: Where is your family from, and what language would you like to use, spoken and written?
Who do you want involved in decisions, and is there anyone you do not want involved?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it to you, and has it helped or got in the way?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
What has helped you and your family so far: faith, relatives, community groups, others?
Are there other kinds of care or healing you or your family use that you would like me to know about?
Would you like an interpreter? If so, which language or sign language, and is there anything I should know about who interprets?
Is there anything you want to know about what happens to the information you give me, including who sees it?
Would it help to talk with other Spanish-speaking parents or disabled people, or would you rather not?
Do you prefer "disabled person", "person with a disability", "persona con discapacidad", or other words?

context.heading: What one study asked about faith
body: Skinner, Correa, Skinner and Bailey (2001) interviewed 250 U.S. parents of Mexican and Puerto Rican origin with young children with developmental delays. Most saw themselves as religious, and most found both their church and their faith supportive, with faith giving more support. Levels of support varied and changed after parents learned of their child's condition. The researchers describe religious frameworks that parents used to make sense of a child's disability. Only the abstract was available, and it does not list those frameworks, so none is offered here as typical.

This study is over 20 years old and is about parents, not disabled adults. It says nothing about any one family, and a family's faith does not tell you what they think about medical care. Ask. Involve a congregation only if the person wants that.

sources.label: Skinner, Correa, Skinner and Bailey, American Journal on Mental Retardation (2001), abstract
Skinner, Rodriguez and Bailey, Journal of Early Intervention (1999), abstract

context.heading: Family and who decides
body: Ayón, Marsiglia and Bermudez-Parsai (2010) studied 150 youth and parent pairs in a metropolitan area near the U.S.–Mexico border, nearly all of Mexican descent. Stronger reported family loyalty and support was linked to fewer symptoms such as depression and anxiety in both youth and parents. It did not cancel out the effects of discrimination. This is mental health research, not disability research, and it does not describe any particular family.

Some people want several relatives involved, and some do not. Adults make their own decisions, with support if they choose it, whatever the family arrangement. Ask each person, and hear from the person directly even if a relative speaks first.

sources.label: Ayón, Marsiglia and Bermudez-Parsai, Journal of Community Psychology (2010)

context.heading: Language, interpreters and words
body: Conchita Hernández Legorreta, profiled on this page, writes that language barriers and inaccessible information kept her parents from advocating for her, and that she often translated her own school paperwork as a child. Use qualified interpreters, not children or relatives, for anything about services, rights or consent.

Do not assume Spanish. Spanish may not be a person's first language, so ask about Indigenous languages. Ask Deaf people which sign language they use; do not assume ASL. Give written material in plain Spanish where Spanish is wanted, along with a phone or in-person follow-up, since not everyone reads documents easily.

No published list of Spanish words to avoid could be confirmed, so none is offered. Hernández Legorreta uses both "blind" and "Latinx & Disabled" for herself, and the Minnesota organization d.a.c. uses "discapacitados" in its own name. Follow the person's lead.

sources.label: GW Graduate School of Education and Human Development, I Grew Up Latinx & Disabled
discapacitados abriéndose caminos

context.heading: Fear of systems, and what comes from institutions
body: Hernández Legorreta rejects the idea that Latino communities are more ableist than others, and says the barriers come mainly from institutions. She has also written about her own undocumented experience. Check system explanations such as language access, hours and paperwork before reading a missed step as cultural.

Immigration enforcement is part of the current setting. In 2025 Mercado Central vendors told Sahan Journal that it had reduced foot traffic and sales. In June 2026 the Minnesota Women's Press reported that Neighborhood House made more than 4,500 food deliveries to 734 families during Operation Metro Surge. Explain in plain language what information is required, who sees it and how it is used. Do not ask about immigration status you do not need, and point people to legal help instead of advising on immigration yourself.

Sahan Journal, Mercado Central and the city's 2025 loan forgiveness
Minnesota Women's Press, Neighborhood House celebrates its 100-plus-year commitment (2026)

context.heading: Peer support, and what could not be found
body: In 2023 HACER and the Southeastern Minnesota Center for Independent Living ran focus groups on the unmet needs of Latino people with disabilities and their caregivers in eleven southeastern counties. The announcement reports no findings. In 2024 the state funded Spanish-language parent support led by Latino staff through PACER Center.

No standing Minnesota organization led by Latino disabled people was found, and no verified Minnesota sources on stigma or on traditional healing. Studies of stigma exist, but only their abstracts were available, so no findings from them are offered. Ask about these things openly and without judgment, and offer peer support as a choice, not a requirement.

PACER Center, press release (July 17, 2024)

organizations.intro: A 2026 state budget profile of the Minnesota Council on Latino Affairs puts the state's Latino population at about 381,000, or about 6.6 percent of all residents; it names no data year or survey, and it says the largest groups trace their heritage to Mexico, Puerto Rico, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala and Colombia. Organizations below include large service agencies, business and research groups, worker and neighborhood organizing, parishes, a state council and Spanish-language media. These are starting points for learning. The list is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts. Check what an organization offers now before making a referral.
